itinerary.cal: Holden Village has been closed to vehicles and hikers due to storm damage through at least summer 2026 - confirm current access status and the Lady of the Lake boat/shuttle schedule before planning this trip, since the return connection is a tight same-day window.

days.note: Access to this remote Glacier Peak Wilderness peak starts with the Lady of the Lake passenger ferry from Chelan to Lucerne, then a shuttle bus to Holden Village. From there it's an 8+ mile trail hike up Railroad Creek to camp at Lower Lyman Lake, gaining about 2,400 ft.

days.note: An early alpine start from Lyman Lakes camp beats the afternoon thunderstorms this exposed ridge is prone to in summer. Hike up to Cloudy Pass, then leave trail to gain the class 2+ East Ridge, skirting old mine workings near Magnolia Mine before following the ridge crest to the summit.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day, ~25-mile round-trip backpack requiring boat + shuttle access to Holden Village, with one full day scrambling the exposed class 2+ East Ridge from a Lyman Lakes base camp (~4,500 ft total gain).

weather.typical: Typical dry North Cascades summer/early-fall pattern for this east-of-crest basin; expect warm days and cool nights with the usual maritime-influenced instability possible
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms and isolated convective weather are possible in August, as is common across the Cascades - carry an early start and turnaround plan

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Consequence is primarily from loose footing and rockfall on scree/talus rather than sheer exposure; a slip on the summit ridge or steep scree sections could still result in a serious fall, and the remote boat-only/multi-day access magnifies the consequence of any injury given the distance from help

avalanche.zone: N/A - dry-season scramble route; no NWAC forecast zone specifically issued during the Late July-September climbing window (avalanche forecasting for the broader Chelan/Glacier Peak Wilderness area, when active in winter/spring, falls loosely under NWAC's East Slopes Central zone, but that does not apply to this route's season)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; this is a talus/heather scramble to the summit ridge

before.approach: Standard approach is via Holden Village: Lady of the Lake ferry from Chelan or Fields Point Landing to Lucerne, shuttle to Holden, then roughly 16 miles up the Railroad Creek Trail to Lyman Lake. As of 2026, Holden Village and Forest Road 8301 are closed to all hikers and vehicles due to 2025 flood/landslide damage, with reopening not expected before 2027 at the earliest — the only current access to Lyman Lake is the longer Phelps Creek Trailhead approach over Spider Gap (roughly 11–12 miles one-way, glacier travel with ice axe required).

Park at the Eagle Creek/Oval trailhead (~3,000 ft) at the end of FR 4420-080, reached via Twisp River Road/FR 44 (~12.5 mi west of Twisp) and the West Buttermilk/FR 4420 spur. From the trailhead, follow Eagle Creek Trail #410 for about 1.5 miles up the Eagle Creek valley (trail parallels the creek, so water is available) to the signed junction with Oval Creek Trail #410A. Bear onto #410A and climb steadily through forest along Oval Creek for roughly 6 more miles, passing West Oval Lake before reaching Middle Oval Lake (~6,700-6,800 ft) — about 7.5 miles and ~3,700 ft of gain from the car; there is good established camping near the lake's outflow if splitting the trip over two days. From the outflow, leave the maintained tread and scramble cross-country up open talus/scree slopes to the north/northeast to gain the Sawtooth crest at a broad saddle roughly 1,200-1,500 ft above the lake, then follow the rocky crest generally north/northwest over blocky, sometimes loose talus to Oval Peak's summit block. Much of this basin burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire, so the lower trail is exposed, dry, and dusty in summer with sections of soft/fragile burned ground that can give way underfoot — carry all the water you'll need once you leave Middle Oval Lake, since there are no reliable sources higher up. The crest scramble is class 2 but has real route-finding and loose-rock exposure in poor visibility.

approach_variants.name: Oval Creek trail to Middle Oval Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the Eagle Creek road end, a mile and a half of valley trail reaches the Oval Creek fork, and six or so more miles of steady forest and old burn lead past the lower lake to Middle Oval Lake at just under 7,000 ft. There is established camping at the outflow, and splitting the trip in two there is the usual plan. Much of the lower basin burned and the tread is dry, dusty and shadeless with sections of soft ground that give underfoot. Carry everything you will drink above the lake — there is nothing reliable higher. Early in the season the Eagle and Oval Creek crossings run high and cold. There is no single defined line up this peak so much as several interchangeable ridge and slope options that converge near the top, and parties commonly go up one and down another for better footing.
approach_variants.season: July to early October; best Aug-Sep
hazards: Loose talus and large slick boulders across the whole upper mountain — twisted-ankle terrain rather than technical
Rockfall from parties above and from blocks that shift underfoot
Several similar-looking gullies and ribs near the summit, hard to tell apart in cloud
High, cold creek crossings during early-season snowmelt
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above treeline
No reliable water above the lakes
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is the outflow of Middle Oval Lake, and it is obvious on the ground: the maintained tread simply ends at the lake outlet, where there is an established stock and backpacker camp on flat ground beside the water. That end of tread is your marker — if you are still on constructed trail you have not started. From the outflow, climb north and northeast up open heather and talus toward the broad saddle on the crest roughly 1,000 to 1,500 ft above the lake, then follow the crest generally north-northwest over blocky ground to the summit block. The summit is not visible from the lake, which is why the gullies matter: several look equally reasonable from below and only one crest line leads cleanly through. The one to refuse outright is the boulder field and gully on the peak's east side, which is dangerously loose and is not a shortcut in either direction. If the crest you are on starts trending east rather than north-northwest, drop back to the saddle and start again.

before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb/scramble back along the Sawtooth crest talus to the saddle above Middle Oval Lake, then drop the scramble slope back down to the lake's outflow and rejoin the maintained Oval Creek Trail #410A. Retrace the ~7.5 miles down through the Oval Lakes basin (past West Oval Lake) to the junction with Eagle Creek Trail #410, and follow that 1.5 miles back to the trailhead. This is a class 2 talus/scree walk-down with no technical rappelling required in either direction — the main descent hazards are loose blocky talus on the crest (twisted-ankle/rockfall terrain, especially with other parties below) and the fragile burned tread lower on the trail. rappels: 0.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Entiat River/Cottonwood Camp Trailhead

before.beta: Pinnacle's standard route gains the peak's west-southwest scree-and-talus facade (the gentle side, opposite the precipitous, largely unclimbed east face). Most parties backpack in 9-13 miles through the North Fork Entiat/Snow Brushy Creek drainage to a high basin camp near Saska Pass, then day-trip the summit via Borealis Pass. The final roughly 800 ft to the top is unroped class 2-3 scree and ridge scrambling with no technical climbing; it is very commonly combined with nearby Saska Peak and/or Emerald Peak from the same camp.
before.turnaround: Given the long approach and afternoon-thunderstorm risk typical of North Cascades summers, set a firm turnaround time before leaving camp or Borealis Pass and hold to it — the loose scree and burned, deadfall-choked trail sections are slow and hazardous to negotiate after dark or in a storm.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep, loose scree ascending/traversing north from the saddle below Borealis Pass toward the base of Pinnacle's summit ridge.
Final summit ridge: mostly easy scrambling over blocky granite with a few short class 2-3 moves to the true summit.

before.rope_note: Class 2-3 off-trail ridge/talus scramble from Borealis Pass; no rope used on standard route.

itinerary.cal: Access is via ~38 miles of FS Road 51 from the town of Entiat; go after the road and high country are snow-free (typically July-October) and note this is Glacier Peak Wilderness, so wilderness group-size/camping rules apply.

days.note: From the Entiat River Trailhead, follow the Entiat River Trail then climb toward Emerald Park and the Saska/Borealis Ridge area, gaining most of the day's elevation in the final push above treeline. Parties describe this as a long, ~10-11 hour carry with a full pack; camp is pitched wherever water and a flat spot align (common sites: ~6,900 ft basin below Emerald Peak, or up on the ~7,600 ft Borealis Ridge crest for a shorter summit day).

days.note: An early, light-pack scramble to the summit and back to camp, followed by breaking camp and hiking all the way out the same day — reported as a very long ~10-11 hour, ~15-mile day but the standard way solo/2-day parties do it. The climb itself is an easy Class 2 walk/scramble on the south slopes from the Saska/Borealis saddle, though loose scree and talus make the last stretch tedious.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high - approach combines roughly 38 miles of driving to the Entiat River Trailhead with a long trail approach (Entiat River / Emerald Park) plus off-trail travel to the peak's base; many parties treat this as a multi-day trip with a backcountry camp
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/backpacking load (roughly 30-40+ lb) typical since the approach length usually favors camping near the peak's base rather than a single-push day

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - multi-day approach is typical; Entiat River Trail and Emerald Park approach cover significant mileage with blowdown reported in some years before off-trail travel to the base of the scramble
requiredSkills: off-trail navigation and route-finding in remote alpine terrain
backcountry/wilderness camping and self-sufficient trip planning
sound judgment on early-season snow if attempting before mid-July
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced scrambler comfortable with sustained Class 3 terrain, loose rock, and off-trail alpine route-finding; not a beginner objective given the remote approach

before.beta: From the Libby Lake Trailhead, hike the well-graded Libby Creek/Libby Lake Trail roughly 5.1–5.5 miles and about 3,185–3,210 ft of gain to Libby Lake (~7,618–7,640 ft). From the lake, locate the loose talus gully that accesses the east-west-oriented ridge (some parties report two gully options near the lake's south end; the standard line rises about 900 ft). The gully is loose and rockfall-prone — favor the climber's-left wall for firmer rock and to reduce hazard to parties below. Once on the ridge crest, an exposed Class 2–3 scramble of roughly half a mile leads toward the summit block, which has a short, unavoidable, no-fall Class 4 move (some reports mention a small tunnel feature en route). USGS topo maps mislabel the western "Libby" summit as the high point (8,580 ft); the true, higher summit is the eastern peak at 8,572 ft. A separate, lower sub-summit called "Corax" (~8,380 ft) sits just west of the main summit saddle. Strong parties often continue the ridge traverse north to Hoodoo Peak, which adds a long exposed Class 4 section and a 5.7 overhanging boulder problem best protected with a short rope.
before.itinerary: Most parties climb Raven Ridge as a single long day from the Libby Lake Trailhead (roughly 10–11 miles round trip with about 4,100+ ft of gain). Parties combining Raven Ridge with Hoodoo Peak often backpack in about 5 miles to camp near the old cabin (~7,170 ft) or at Libby Lake, climb both peaks via the connecting ridge on day two, and hike out on day three (or as a very long single day for fit, fast parties).

access.fees: The Forest Service states that no parking fee or pass is required at the Libby Lake Trailhead, though some parties report that a Northwest Forest Pass is expected — confirm current signage locally
access.permit: No wilderness permit is required for day or overnight travel in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness
access.closures: No permanent closures reported; the trail carries fire damage (burned root holes) from the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire between roughly miles 0.8 and 2.5; the route is generally snowbound and inaccessible from about November through May
access.landManager: USDA Forest Service, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District
access.passRequired: Conflicting reports — the Forest Service says none is required at Libby Lake Trailhead, but a Northwest Forest Pass is also reported as needed

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead registration box. Most trailheads also need a Northwest Forest Pass to park.
